name: Bianca Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. I don't usually do surveys, but my mum said I should. Ask away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on our family farm with my mum and dad, outside the village on the old Station Road. We've got about 120 outdoor sows, wheat and potatoes on around 200 hectares. I'm up at six feeding the pigs, checking water and farrowing huts, then whatever the season needs: drilling, spraying, potato harvest. I like the pigs best; the potato harvest in October is just cold, wet and long.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Dan in the cottage at the end of the farm track, and he drives a feed lorry for the merchant in town. I've got a third share in the land, which Dad set up last year, plus savings from not paying much rent. I don't use AI at all; Dad does the forms on the computer and I don't want to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I never believed the fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: farming carries on, people have to eat. My pigs don't care what the computers can do, and neither does the potato harvest. I don't post online, so I'd just say it to Dan and the lads at the merchant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means life carries on and I'm glad. I've got a share of the land, a decent wage from the farm and a cheap house. Pig prices go up and down, that's the only real worry, and that's been true for a hundred years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep feeding the pigs, keep saving, keep out of Dad's computer. Maybe Dad would use AI for the subsidy forms and that's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. Like a Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned pig prices. When did they last hurt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago we lost money on every pig for about eight months. We got through on savings and the potato crop. That's farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try AI if it turned out to be small and simple?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if Dad showed me something that saved a whole day. But I'd want to see it working for a year first.

say: I'd tell Dan that **farming carries on** because people have to eat.
I'd say my **pigs** and potatoes don't care what computers can do.
think: Privately my **land share**, wage and cheap house make life feel secure.
The only real worry is **pig prices**, which have always gone up and down.
do: Keep feeding the **sows** and running the farm as normal.
Leave the **subsidy forms** and any AI to Dad.
feel: I feel **calm**, like an ordinary Tuesday.
S0.quote: My pigs don't care what the computers can do, and neither does the potato harvest.
fieldNote: She's **plainly resistant** to tech but not hostile, and leaves it to her father.
Her security rests on **land ownership** and a cheap home.
She treats **price swings** as normal farming risk.

steps.text: Keep feeding the sows and running Costa Farm as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds more realistic. The office lot get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mainly a desk thing and farmers will be fine for a while. I'd say if machines take over the boring office work, that's their business. I've never typed a question into an AI in my life, and I've still got more work than hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm a bit worried about Dan. Not the driving, that's hands-on, but the merchant could use AI to plan routes and cut a driver. My own work feels safe for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal on the farm. I'd tell Dan to keep his head down and be the driver they can't do without. If robots for pigs started appearing, I'd wait and see how they worked on other farms first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me, for Dan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if Dan lost his job at the merchant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan could drive for someone else, there's always lorry work round here. Or he'd come and work on the farm, which Dad would love and I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you hate it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because then all our eggs are in one basket. If the farm has a bad year, we'd both have a bad year.

say: I'd say it's mainly a **desk thing**, and farmers will be fine for a while.
I'd say I've **never used AI** and still have more work than hours.
think: Privately my **own work** feels safe for years.
I'm a bit worried the merchant uses AI **route planning** to cut a driver like Dan.
do: Carry on as normal on the **family farm**.
Wait and see how **pig robots** work on other farms before considering any.
feel: I feel **a bit uneasy**, mostly for Dan.
S1.quote: I've never typed a question into an AI in my life, and I've still got more work than hours.
fieldNote: Her unease is about the **household**, through Dan's job, not her own.
She doesn't want all income in **one basket**, a pragmatic centre view.
She defers any change until it's **proven elsewhere**.

steps.text: Carry on running the pig unit and potatoes as normal
Watch how pig robots do on other farms before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's not much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to sort this out, because ordinary people can't. I wouldn't be on a soapbox; I'd just say it at the pub. I'd say nobody asked for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the farm becomes a robot business or it dies. My boyfriend Dan drives a feed lorry and I muck out pigs, so in this picture we'd both be waiting for the same robot van. Dad's sixty, and he'd want to buy the robots and I'd be the one standing there not knowing how they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending on anything we don't need, like the new quad bike we'd planned. I'd talk to Mum and Dad about whether we sell the sows before 2031, because the big pig farms will have robots and undercut us. Dan and I would put off buying the bigger house in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A knot in my stomach. I'd go quiet, Dan says that's how he can tell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a land share. Doesn't that protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It protects the land, not my job. Owning a third of the land won't feed me if a robot can do my third of the work. I'd still be thirty-one, owning dirt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum and Dad, and they'd lean on me. Dan's family are all in the city, so it's our lot or nobody.

say: I'd say at the pub that the **government** has to sort this, because ordinary people can't.
think: Privately the farm becomes a **robot business** or it dies.
My **land share** protects the land, not my own work.
do: Cancel the planned **quad bike** and stop other spending.
Talk to Mum and Dad about selling the **sows** before 2031.
Put off buying the **bigger house** in town with Dan.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with a knot in my stomach.
I go **quiet**, which is how Dan can tell.
S2.quote: My boyfriend Dan drives a feed lorry and I muck out pigs, so in this picture we'd both be waiting for the same robot van.
fieldNote: She sees both household jobs, **pig work** and **lorry driving**, falling to robots together.
Her land is a **real cushion**, but she knows it doesn't replace a wage.
She'd **lean on family**, which matches her centre, practical outlook.

steps.text: Cancel the new quad bike and other planned spending
Ask Mum and Dad about selling the sows before 2031
Put off buying the bigger house in town with Dan
Pool money and work with Mum and Dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, and eight for the robots. Better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for farms to adjust, so let's not panic. I'd tell the lads at the merchant to keep an eye on the news. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I still don't want to learn the robots. If the robots come in 2034, I'd rather sell the sows in 2032 than buy a machine I don't understand. We'd keep the arable and hire a contractor with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, I'd just keep going and save harder, maybe an extra five hundred a month. Around 2031, when the thinking AI arrives, I'd see what pig prices do. If they crash, we sell the sows and I'd find work on a farm that still uses people, or help Dad with the arable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but slower. Like knowing a big bill is due in the spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad would want the robots. What happens if you disagree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad and I would argue, like we did about the new grain dryer. He'd probably win, and I'd sulk for a month and then do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most if the sows went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farrowing. Seeing a sow with twelve piglets in the straw. No robot is going to enjoy that.

say: I'd say there's **time to adjust**, so let's not panic.
I'd tell the lads at the merchant to **watch the news**.
think: Privately I'd rather **sell the sows** than learn a robot I don't understand.
We'd keep the **arable** and hire a contractor with machines.
do: Save an extra **five hundred** a month from now.
Watch **pig prices** around 2031 before deciding anything.
Sell the sows if prices **crash**, and work the arable.
feel: I feel **anxious** but slower, like a bill due in spring.
S3.quote: If the robots come in 2034, I'd rather sell the sows in 2032 than buy a machine I don't understand.
fieldNote: More time doesn't change her choice; she'd rather **exit pigs** than adopt robots.
She expects a **family argument** with her father and expects to lose it.
Her love of the **farrowing** shows what she'd lose beyond money.

steps.text: Save an extra five hundred a month starting now
Watch pig prices around 2031 before making changes
Sell the sows if pig prices crash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and farmers have been through worse. I'd say that to anyone who asked, which wouldn't be many people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I wouldn't do much for a long while. Ten years is a long time on a farm; my dad has changed his mind about the potatoes three times in ten years. By then I'll know if I'm running the farm or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as we do now and keep saving. I'd let Dad decide about robots in a few years, when they're cheap and proven. If Dan wanted to, we'd look at the bigger house again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but mostly fine. It's on my mind in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd start now, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit of training on the new farm software, if Dad pushed. But not this year. Next year, perhaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know when it's time to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the neighbours start buying robots and making money. Then I'd know it's real.

say: I'd say there's **plenty of time** and farmers have survived worse.
I'd say it to the **few people** who asked.
think: Privately I wouldn't change much for a **long while**.
By the time robots come I'll know whether I'm **running the farm**.
do: Keep **farming** as we do now and keep saving.
Let **Dad decide** on robots once they're cheap and proven.
Look again at the **bigger house** with Dan.
feel: I feel **a little uneasy**, mostly fine.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time on a farm; my dad has changed his mind about the potatoes three times in ten years.
fieldNote: Her trigger to act is **neighbours** making money from robots, not news.
She **delegates** tech decisions to her father.
The long timeline lets **family plans** like the house come back.

steps.text: Keep the sows and potatoes going as now
Wait until neighbours profit from robots before acting
Revisit buying the bigger house in town with Dan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. Dan and I would both lose our work around the same time and I'd be stuck with a farm I can't run the new way. What would help is someone teaching farmers the robots slowly, and a grant so small farms aren't swallowed by big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the parents. Lots of us young ones are on family farms, and it's our dads who'd make the call, not us.

headlineQuote: Owning a third of the land won't feed me if a robot can do my third of the work.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old** who works her family's pig, wheat and potato farm.
She has a **third share** of the land and lives with Dan, a feed lorry driver.
She **never uses AI** and leaves computers to her father.
She's **calm** in mild pictures and **anxious** in AGI ones, fearing both household jobs go.
Her plan is to **exit pigs** rather than learn robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, since she and Dan could lose work at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **slow, hands-on training** in farm robots.
She wants **grants** so small farms aren't swallowed by big ones.
